soil-chem-076.title: The chemistry hidden in a handful of soil
soil-chem-076.text: Nine-tenths of a soil's weight is rock-born. Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil. Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and those characteristics depend on three things: mineral composition, soil organic matter and environmental factors. Plants take part too. They trade the elements they feed on with microorganisms, and they absorb them. That creates concentration gradients of cations and anions, the positively and negatively charged ions. Each of these elements follows its own cycle through rock, air, water and life. Nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock. The field has a founder. In the early 1870s J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions. He is considered the father of soil chemistry. Until the late 1960s the questions stayed close to the farm: the reactions behind soil formation and plant growth. On farms today the chemistry still serves plant feeding, the fertility of soil and the ingredients farmers spread to feed crops. Concern over pollution then shifted the field toward the environment, the turn traced in {{ref:soil-chem-077}}.

soil-chem-079.title: Clay minerals, the sheet silicates born of water
soil-chem-079.text: For a long time clay looked like ordinary rock ground very fine. Only with X-ray diffraction in the 1930s did it prove to be mainly sheet silicates formed as secondary minerals, not tiny grains of quartz, feldspar or mica. A clay mineral is a hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a silicate built in sheets that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations. Its structure rests on flat hexagonal sheets like those of the mica minerals. Water is essential. Clay minerals form in its presence, as common products of {{ref:soil-found-052}}, including the weathering of feldspar, and of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration. That need for water makes them rare in the Solar System, though they have been detected on Mars, Ceres and other bodies. On Earth they are very common in soils and in fine-grained rocks such as shale, mudstone, siltstone, slate and phyllite. In a soil they never stop forming. For as long as the soil exists, new clay arises by inheritance, by neoformation or by transformation of earlier minerals. Most soil clays are crystalline, but some are amorphous. A soil's clay is a mixture of types, often with one dominating according to the kind of soil. The charges on clay minerals matter for crops. With soil organic matter, they supply most of a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, its power to hold cations that plants feed on, such as potassium and ammonium.

soil-chem-107.title: Diatomaceous earth, a powder of fossil shells
soil-chem-107.text: Diatomaceous earth is a rock made of fossils. Also called diatomite or kieselgur, this soft sedimentary rock crumbles into a fine white powder. It is the silica shells of diatoms, piled up in lake or marine sediments over millions of years, and is usually 80–90% silica. Its particles are typically 10 to 200 μm, and high porosity makes the powder light. FAO soil description lists it among the materials of limnic L layers. Gardeners use it as a bonsai medium and conditioner: like {{ref:soil-fert-072}}, it holds water yet drains freely.

soil-chem-104.title: Goethite, the iron mineral in rust and yellow soils
soil-chem-104.text: Every patch of rust holds a soil mineral. Goethite is the α form of the iron(III) oxide-hydroxide FeO(OH). It is the main component of rust and of bog iron ore, which forms in swampy ground at the head of springs. In soil it often forms by weathering of other iron-rich minerals. As iron-bearing minerals reach the soil's oxidation zone, ferrous iron(II) becomes ferric iron(III). The parent mineral's shape is kept, so goethite often forms pseudomorphs, crystals in another mineral's outline. Some bacteria make it too. It is concentrated in {{ref:soil-form-065}}, alongside quartz and other iron and clay minerals. Goethite is yellowish to reddish to dark brown or black, and it helps tint soils yellow to red. Its grip on nutrients is fierce: clays rich in goethite hold phosphorus so tightly that plants cannot absorb it. Heating converts it to maghemite, which raises soil magnetism. Long used as the pigment brown ochre, it was first described in 1806 and named after Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

soil-chem-080.title: Two kinds of sheet that build every clay
soil-chem-080.text: Every clay mineral, however varied, is assembled from just two kinds of sheet. The tetrahedral sheet is made of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron shares three oxygens with its neighbors in a hexagonal array. The fourth, apical oxygen points the same way on every tetrahedron. The octahedral sheet holds small cations such as aluminium or magnesium, each surrounded by six oxygens. The apical oxygens also form one face of the octahedral sheet, which locks the two together. An extra oxygen above each hexagonal gap bonds to hydrogen as a hydroxyl group. Fitting them together corrugates the tetrahedral sheet and flattens the octahedral one. The clay in {{ref:soil-chem-088}} shows the shorthand: its T sheet holds silicon among four oxygens, its O sheet aluminium among six oxygens or hydroxyls. Depending on composition, a finished layer is neutral or carries a net negative charge. Interlayer cations such as Na+ or K+ balance that charge, or a lone octahedral sheet does. A clay crystal is a stack of these layers separated by interlayers.

soil-chem-081.title: One-to-one or two-to-one: how clay sheets stack
soil-chem-081.text: Clay mineralogists sort their subjects with two numbers. A 1:1 clay builds each layer from one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet. A 2:1 clay places an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets. That difference decides how the layers hold together. 1:1 layers carry no charge and cling to each other by hydrogen bonds. 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge, so something positive must bind them. In some groups that is a scatter of cations; in others, a whole octahedral sheet. Four main groups result. The kaolin group, typified by {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, also holds dickite, {{ref:soil-chem-090}} and nacrite, all 1:1 clays like serpentine. The 2:1 groups are three. {{ref:soil-chem-091}} includes {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, nontronite, beidellite and saponite, and its layers are bound by cations. So are those of {{ref:soil-chem-094}}. {{ref:soil-chem-087}} is bound by octahedral sheets instead. Talc and {{ref:soil-chem-095}} are 2:1 clays too. Soil scientists usually give the same four groups for soils. Some clays break the pattern. {{ref:soil-chem-110}} and sepiolite are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure. Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, either randomly, coded R0, or in order. Perfectly ordered R1 mixes have their own names, such as rectorite and corrensite.

soil-chem-095.title: Vermiculite, the clay named for breeding worms
soil-chem-095.text: Heat vermiculite and it exfoliates, splitting and swelling apart. That habit gave the mineral its name, from the Latin vermiculare, 'to breed worms', when it was first described in 1824 at Millbury, Massachusetts. Vermiculite is a hydrous 2:1 clay mineral. It forms by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of two micas, biotite and phlogopite. These lose the potassium between their sheets, and magnesium and iron take its place. Hydrated magnesium holds the crystals loosely, so vermiculite swells, though less than {{ref:soil-chem-093}}. That makes it a limited-expansion clay with a medium shrink–swell capacity. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} of 100–150 meq/100 g, milliequivalents per 100 grams, is high, above that of the clays in {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. It occurs interlayered with biotite, phlogopite and {{ref:soil-chem-087}}, typically where felsic rocks meet mafic or ultramafic ones. Pure vermiculite contains no asbestos. Ore from some deposits, notably the Libby mine in Montana, was contaminated, and some products contained asbestos until the early 1990s.

soil-chem-088.title: Kaolinite, the white clay of china and the tropics
soil-chem-088.text: Paper, porcelain and hot, wet soils share one clay. Kaolinite, also called kaolin, is a common 1:1 clay mineral, Al2Si2O5(OH)4. Soft, earthy and usually white, it forms by chemical weathering of aluminium silicates such as feldspar. Each layer bonds a silica tetrahedral sheet to an aluminium octahedral sheet. Tight hydrogen bonds hold successive layers together, so water cannot get between them, so kaolinite does not swell and has a low shrink–swell capacity. The layers carry no net charge, so no large cations sit between them, hence its low {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, just 1–15 meq/100 g. Its surfaces often carry positive charges instead. Moist, it is plastic: a film of water binds its plate-like crystals yet lets them slip. Dried, it is rigid but fragile. Kaolinite abounds in soils formed by chemical weathering in hot, moist climates. The INERA classification calls soils whose clay is mostly kaolinite kaolisols. Rock rich in it is kaolin or china clay, an industrial raw material used above all for paper and ceramics.

soil-chem-094.title: Illite, the potassium clay that will not swell
soil-chem-094.text: Illite is the only clay mineral that contains potassium, and that potassium shapes its character. Also called hydromica, it is a group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, structurally close to the mica muscovite. Poorly hydrated potassium ions fill the space between its layers and bind them strongly, so illite does not swell. Those bonds also shrink its active surface. What little swelling it shows depends on how far potassium feldspar has weathered. Its {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, typically 20–30 meq/100 g, is higher than kaolinite's but lower than that of {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Illite forms by alteration of muscovite and feldspar in weathering and hydrothermal settings, and from swelling clays exposed to potassium-rich groundwater. It is common in sediments, soils and argillaceous rocks, and its share of soil clay rises relative to kaolinite toward cooler climates. It was first described in 1937 from the Maquoketa shale of Calhoun County, Illinois, and named after the state.

soil-chem-105.title: Gibbsite, what remains when silica is gone
soil-chem-105.text: Strip a clay of its silica and gibbsite is what remains. Gibbsite is a mineral form of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3. It is built of stacked sheets of linked octahedra, each an aluminium ion bonded to six hydroxide groups, with a third of the octahedral sites left empty. Each sheet is electrically neutral, so no ions glue the sheets together. Only weak residual bonds hold them, which makes gibbsite very soft and easily cleaved. Identical aluminium hydroxide 'gibbsite layers' sit sandwiched between silicate sheets in the illite, kaolinite and {{ref:soil-chem-091}} clay groups. Gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals, and {{ref:soil-chem-097}} alters to it where silica is removed. Where heavy rainfall leaches most silica from alumino-silica clays, it is among the less soluble oxides left behind, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils. As one of the three main phases of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}, it is an important aluminium ore. It is named after the American mineral collector George Gibbs (1776–1833).

soil-chem-108.title: Bauxite, the rock behind the world's aluminium
soil-chem-108.text: The world's aluminium comes mainly from one weathered rock. Bauxite is a sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content. It consists mostly of gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore, mixed with goethite, {{ref:soil-chem-112}}, kaolinite and a little anatase. Lateritic bauxites, found mostly in the tropics, form by lateritization of silicate rocks such as granite, gneiss, basalt and shale. Karst bauxites lie over limestone and dolomite. Bauxite needs even more intense weathering and better drainage than iron-rich laterites. Those conditions dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite. Most deposits lie within 1 to 20 metres of the surface, so bauxite is usually strip mined.

soil-chem-077.title: What becomes of a pollutant once it reaches soil
soil-chem-077.text: A chemical spilled on soil does not simply sit there. Environmental soil chemistry studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them. Adsorption and desorption, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can each raise or lower a chemical's toxicity. Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though clean-up engineers often disregard them. The field grew from worry, since the late 1960s, about pollution and its ecological and health risks.

soil-chem-078.title: How soil chemists test a sample without spoiling it
soil-chem-078.text: Drying a soil sample changes the very chemistry under study. Air-drying at about 25 °C and sieving to 2 mm markedly disrupt structure, microbial life and properties tied to pH. Many chemists now keep samples, taken from undisturbed horizons, field-moist at 4 °C. In batch equilibration, a solution of known ion content is shaken with soil, say 25 mL with 5 g. The liquid is then analyzed for mg of ion per g of soil. Column studies leach a solution through soil at a controlled rate, mimicking rain and snowmelt. Surface spectroscopy, such as infrared or X-ray methods, shows how ions bind to particles without disturbing the soil.

soil-chem-084.title: Soil colloids, the tiny particles that do the chemistry
soil-chem-084.text: Most of a soil's chemistry happens on particles too small to see. Soil colloids, chiefly clay and the dark decayed material called {{ref:soil-bio-089}}, have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 1 μm. Their charged surfaces hold ions and trade them with the soil water. Clay, a colloidal and usually crystalline phyllosilicate, is the most active mineral part of soil. It owes that to its high specific surface area and its unbalanced negative charges. Negative charges on colloids hold cations, and positive charges hold anions. Together they give soil its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-053}}. This exchange does quiet, constant work. It buffers soil pH, alters structure and purifies percolating water by adsorbing cations, both useful and harmful. Soil clays fall into four kinds: layered alumino-silica clays, crystalline chain carbonates and sulfates, young {{ref:soil-chem-099}}, and old, highly leached {{ref:soil-chem-106}}. The organic colloids are richer still: on a dry-weight basis their exchange capacity is many times that of clay. Climate can strip colloids away. In tropical rainforests, heat and heavy rain largely destroy clay and organic colloids, leaving only oxide clays that hold few cations.

soil-chem-112.title: Hematite, the blood-red oxide of old soils
soil-chem-112.text: Hematite takes its name from the Greek for blood. It is a common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils. Clay-sized hematite forms as a secondary mineral during soil weathering. With goethite and other iron oxides, it gives many tropical, ancient or highly weathered soils their red color. It grows from {{ref:soil-chem-111}}, a metastable precursor of both hematite and goethite. Red ochre is clay colored by 20% to 70% unhydrated hematite. Older ironstone crusts in {{ref:soil-class-137}} contain more hematite and boehmite than plinthite does.

soil-chem-083.title: Did life begin on the surface of clay?
soil-chem-083.text: The first living things may have had help from clay. In 1985 Graham Cairns-Smith proposed that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water. Clay minerals form only where water is present, and many theories of how life began involve them. Laboratory work lends weight to the idea: {{ref:soil-chem-093}} has been shown to catalyze the joining of nucleotides into RNA in water, and the formation of membranes from lipids. In 1998 Hyman Hartman went further. He proposed that the first organisms were self-replicating iron-rich clays that fixed carbon dioxide into oxalic and other dicarboxylic acids.

soil-chem-082.title: Telling one clay from another in the laboratory
soil-chem-082.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study. X-ray diffraction is the main tool for identifying them, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. To put numbers on a soil's clays, analysts first measure its soil organic matter, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals. They then estimate clay percentages from glycol adsorption, {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, K2O and thermal data. Glycol adsorption measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites over eight hours of exposure to the vapor at 60 °C. Illite is estimated from its potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.

soil-chem-087.title: Chlorite, a green clay with no chlorine in it
soil-chem-087.text: Chlorite contains no chlorine; its name is Greek for green. It is a chemically varied group of 2:1 clay minerals. Aluminium replacing silicon gives their layers a negative charge. A positively charged hydroxide sheet of hydrated magnesium, called a brucite sheet, binds the layers, not the scattered cations of vermiculite or mica. With two silicon planes, one aluminium and one magnesium plane, chlorite is described as a 2:2 clay. Water is not adsorbed between its layers, so it does not swell, and its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. A common weathering product found widely in clay, it also forms in low-grade metamorphic rocks.

soil-chem-097.title: Allophane, the shapeless clay of volcanic ash
soil-chem-097.text: Allophane never quite becomes a crystal. This hydrous aluminium silicate has only short-range order, so it counts as a mineraloid. It forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2. Electron micrographs show hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across. Its structure has been debated; one account describes curved alumina and silica layers like those of clays. It alters to {{ref:soil-chem-090}} where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed. It is among the amorphous materials that define the volcanic-ash soils of {{ref:soil-class-092}}.

openers.chem: Soil chemistry is the study of the chemical characteristics of soil, and much of it plays out on surfaces too small to see. Its first actors are the clay minerals: hydrous aluminium silicates built in sheets that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations. Around them sit iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides left by weathering, including the minerals of the world's main source of aluminium. The same chemistry also decides what becomes of contaminants once they are released into soil.
openers.clay-minerals-and-colloids: Every clay mineral is built from just two kinds of sheet. One is made of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra; the other holds small cations such as aluminium or magnesium, each surrounded by six oxygens. How those sheets stack sorts the clays into two families, 1:1 and 2:1, and much follows from that choice. This chapter meets the common clays in turn, from a 1:1 clay also called kaolin to a 2:1 clay that expands greatly when heated. It then turns to the iron and aluminium minerals that weathering leaves beside them, and to a soft rock of fossil silica that crumbles into a fine white powder.
